newsitem.title: ITALY: Opponents round on Italy's separatist Bossi.
newsitem.headline: Opponents round on Italy's separatist Bossi.

text.p: Opponents raised the heat on separatist Umberto Bossi and his drive for an independent north on Thursday, led by a warning from Prime Minister Romano Prodi that Italy must not meet the same fate as Yugoslavia.
The expressions of unease at Northern League leader Bossi's plan to proclaim a "federal republic of Padania" on Sunday marked a shift in tone from a low-key approach to Bossi's move.

They united the centre-left government, the opposition and the Vatican in an assault on a symbolic step the firebrand secessionist says will lead to full independence within a year for the northern powerhouse regions of Italy's economy.

Bossi is due to embark on Friday on a three-day "March to the Sea" along the River Po, with his pilgrimage climaxing in a declaration of independence in Venice. He hopes more than one million followers will flock to the river to mark the event.

Prodi, who has until now played down the secessionist threat, changed the mood on Wednesday night with a warning that while the government would allow peaceful protest it would not tolerate any breach of the law or national unity.

"This is a great country, and it must not meet the same end as Czechoslovakia, or even Yugoslavia," he told RAI television. "Our example is Germany, which is even more united, not those countries which split, bringing grief to all their citizens."

Few, if any, political commentators believe Italians would take up arms for or against a northern breakaway, not least in the absence of the ethnic and religious rivalries that underpinned the bloodshed in former Yugoslavia.
But Prodi's four-month-old government has faced political flak for not taking a tougher stand on Bossi's challenge.

Critics say mockery of Bossi's agenda has played into his hands by seeming to ignore the genuine frustration of northerners with high taxes and central government bureaucracy and the anti-southern prejudice he has jumped on to woo support.

Gianfranco Fini, whose hard-right National Alliance party is strongest in the south, branded Bossi "disgusting" on Thursday, comparing him to a "drug addict who has to boost his dose of insults and provocations by the day".
He called for a huge turnout in Milan on Sunday at a unity march his party will stage as a counter to Bossi's campaign.

PierFerdinando Casini, an ally of Fini's in Italy's main opposition centre-right bloc, said all parties in parliament had to move fast towards federal reform if they intended to cut the ground from under Bossi's feet.
"If we don't, we can issue all the nice condemnations we want but the risk is that Bossi will win the game," he said.

The semi-official Vatican newspaper L'Osservatore Romano also weighed in, criticising League leaflets distributed in northern schools which have called for the expulsion of teachers from Italy's south.

It said the leaflets would foment "dangerous racist phobias among the young" and carried an article by the Archbishop of Milan, Cardinal Carlo Maria Martini, urging Roman Catholics to steer clear of politicians prone to "demagogy and adventurism".
Bossi has been vague about what constitutes "Padania", defining it in social and economic terms -- a yardstick that pits the affluent north against Italy's less developed south.
His lieutenant Roberto Maroni said this week that on those terms the self-styled republic could stretch as far south as the central region of Umbria, knocking at the gates of Rome.

In the absence of ethnic or linguistic rallying calls, Bossi has proved adept at creating a "Padanian" mythology for his followers that ranges from his mystification of the Po, Italy's longest river, to unashamed plagiarism of foreign icons.

He has cited Gandhi as his model for non-violent action, compared himself to 13th century Scotsman William "Braveheart" Wallace and his independence battle and borrowed from the American declaration of independence for Sunday's proclamation.
